title: Deterministic request-id hashing and idempotent-span strategy for retry-heavy endpoints
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Background: Several customer-facing endpoints (batch API, streaming proxy) exhibit high retry churn due to transient network errors and client SDK aggressive retry heuristics. This causes duplicated spans, inflated error rates in dashboards, and noisy traces that make root-cause analysis harder. Current instrumentation attaches a new span per incoming request without a stable deterministic request identifier; retries look like distinct requests.

Goal: Introduce a deterministic request hashing function and an idempotent-span instantiation strategy in our SDK and server middleware so retried requests map to the same top-level trace/span while preserving per-attempt timing (as child attempt spans). This should reduce duplicate trace noise, stabilize error/latency metrics, and make tracing compatible with client-side retries and proxies.

Proposal summary:
- Deterministic request fingerprint: compute a stable 64-bit hex fingerprint from a canonicalized request envelope (method, path, normalized query params, body-sha256 if present, client-provided idempotency-key header when available). Use Blake3-128 truncated to 64 bits for speed.
- Request ID precedence: if client provides X-Request-Id or X-Idempotency-Key, use that as the primary key (hashed to the fingerprint). Otherwise compute fingerprint server-side in middleware.
- Idempotent top-level span: when a request arrives, middleware attempts a non-blocking span lookup in a short-lived in-memory span registry keyed by the fingerprint+route-version. If found and the previous attempt is still open, attach this attempt as a child span labeled attempt-N and link to the existing trace. If not found, create a new top-level span and register it with a short TTL (default 30s) to capture immediate retries.
- Attempt spans: each physical retry (different TCP connection) creates a child attempt span with attempt metadata (attempt_index, transport_error, upstream_status). These are emitted as separate spans but parented under the deterministic top-level span to preserve visibility.
- Backwards compatibility: Fall back to current behavior if tracing backend or sampling decision is not compatible. Respect client-supplied tracing headers (traceparent) and do not override traceids when present.

Design decisions and trade-offs:
- Choice of hash: Blake3 was chosen for speed and small code footprint across languages. Truncating to 64 bits risks collision but the collision window (per route) is acceptable; we add a route-version salt to reduce cross-route collisions.
- In-memory registry: keeps overhead minimal; TTL prevents registry growth. For high fanout endpoints we will introduce sharded registries per worker process to avoid global coordination. We intentionally avoid cross-process persistence (like Redis) to keep latency/cost low; future iteration may add optional persistent dedupe for long-tail retries.
- Sampling interaction: For sampled-out traces, still perform deterministic fingerprinting but avoid creating heavy instrumentation; emit lightweight link metadata so UI can surface aggregated retry counts.

Implementation plan:
- SDK changes (JS, Python, Go): expose helper computeRequestFingerprint(envelope, opts) with opt-in normalization modes. SDKs accept a new header X-RW-Fingerprint when provided by the client to avoid server recomputation.
- Server middleware (proxy and runtime): compute fingerprint if header missing, perform span registry lookup/create logic, attach child attempt spans.
- Telemetry: add dashboard panels to show "retries per fingerprint", "duplicate top-level spans suppressed", and change error-rate math to count unique fingerprints by default in the new latency/error dashboard mode.
- Rollout: opt-in via feature flag for 2 weeks with synthetic load tests. Gradual ramp from 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% across regions, monitoring duplication metrics and span count per trace.

Acceptance criteria:
- 90% reduction in duplicate top-level spans for high-retry synthetic tests.
- No more than 0.5% increase in median request latency introduced by middleware fingerprinting on p50/p95.
- Trace consumer dashboards show stable error rates (duplicates eliminated) in canary runs.

Telemetry/Datapoints to track:
- fingerprinted_requests_total, fingerprinted_retries_total, fingerprint_collision_rate, registry_hit_rate, median_fingerprint_latency_ms.

comments: 2025-10-16 - Maya Chen: Spiked JS helper and measured median compute time ~0.12ms for typical envelope; acceptable for p50 but p95 influenced by large bodies. Added option to skip body hashing when Content-Length > 64KB.

2025-10-21 - Liam Ortega: Backend middleware sketch done. Using a per-worker LRU registry keyed by fingerprint+route-version. Implemented TTL=30s. Initial microbench shows 1.8% CPU regression under synthetic 10k rps test on c4-large worker.

2025-10-24 - PR feedback (runtime#1467): Design review comment from Priya (Trace Team) - ensure we don't break cross-service correlation if client supplied traceparent. Decided: respect traceparent and only apply fingerprinting when traceparent absent or when trace won't be sampled.

2025-10-28 - QA: Ran synthetic retry storms with exponential backoff. Observed 78% reduction in top-level duplicates in single-region canary at 10% rollout. Need to reduce registry CPU cost; experimenting with a compact 16-bit bloom prefilter to short-circuit misses.

2025-11-01 - Security review request submitted: added note to security_review_required in metadata and linked threat model. Key question: could fingerprinting leak PII? We decided to always hash bodies and never log raw canonicalized values; use body-sha256 optional mode to avoid storing body content.

2025-11-02 - Liam Ortega: Merged SDK helper into go and python experimental branches. Preparing canary 1% rollout for next deploy window. Monitoring dashboard configured for collision_rate and registry_hit_rate.
